MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota (CNN) -- David and Christina Macfarlane always dreamed of opening a restaurant. And with David's background as a White House chef, they certainly have the in-house culinary ability. David and Christina Macfarlane in their Minneapolis restaurant, L'Ecosse. But they never imagined they'd be doing it in one of the toughest economic times ever, and they wondered if it would even be possible. "The banks were like, 'You're opening a restaurant now?' " Christina says. " 'Yeah, we're opening a restaurant now.' " David was born in Glasgow, Scotland, but moved to the United States with his family in his early teens and soon found his passion for the palate. Soon after high school, he joined the U.S. Navy, where he ultimately spent years cooking -- two of which were spent in the kitchen at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue as a chef for President Clinton at the beginning of his first term in 1992. Looking at a picture of himself and the former president, David describes a favorite memory. "He said that was the best meal he ever ate. I was pretty geeked about that."  See more about that favorite meal » . But the Macfarlanes wanted more time as a family -- something not suited to David's high-profile job. They moved a number of times before settling down in the Minneapolis, Minnesota, suburbs where, most recently, David worked for Fusion Culinary -- until his position was eliminated, that is. Christina says that as dismayed as David was over the job loss, she saw it as "a blessing." "I thought, 'Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!' " she says, adding that she saw it as the perfect opportunity to follow through with their dream. Now, despite the battered economy, the two stand behind the bar in their new restaurant, L'Ecosse, which, incidentally, is French for "Scotland." However, they have a slightly different take on the menu than perhaps they would have had if times were perkier. "We went to over a dozen restaurants looking at menus, pricepoints, [and] realizing the struggles in the economy," Christina recalls. The two concluded that while people are still eating out, they aren't seeking "fancy" food -- in other words, they weren't seeking the type of fare one might typically associate with state dinners at the White House. David says that's all a misconception anyway. "Comfort food," he says. "That's what the president wanted most." Some of the president's favorite foods, David says were nachos and salsa, tuna sandwiches, or just warm milk and cookies. "[President Clinton] wasn't looking for any of the fancy frou-frou stuff. We did that for state dinners or we did that for dignitaries that would come in, but ... at lunchtime when the president would be in the Oval Office by himself, [he'd say] 'Lemme have a tuna sandwich.' " At L'Ecosse, tuna and warm cookies are on the menu. Keeping with his Scottish upbringing, David's menu also is largely UK-centric: meat pies and fish and chips are two of the specialties. He does it all with fresh, local ingredients and says he can keep prices down because he does a lot of the work himself and with the help of a very minimal staff.  Watch the chef talk about keeping it simple » . Everything on the breakfast and lunch menus is priced under $10, and the two say that when they expand to a full dinner menu once their liquor license is approved, they want to keep prices similarly low. "The reason we did that was so nobody had sticker shock," David says. "They're very good items, but they're also inexpensive items and you're not going to break the bank." "If you want to come in and get Bill Clinton's favorite, it doesn't have to be $15 during the day. And that's what we want people to understand -- we understand where you're at." As Christina puts it, "You are going to get great food that your mother used to make for you." And, ideally, the bill won't send you into debt.

***

**MINNEAPOLIS, Minnesota (CNN)** — Opening a restaurant had always been a lifelong dream for David and Christina Macfarlane. Given David’s background as a former White House chef, the couple certainly possessed the requisite culinary expertise. Yet, standing inside their newly opened Minneapolis establishment, *L'Ecosse*, they admit they never envisioned launching a business during one of the most challenging economic climates in history. The daunting timing left them questioning if it was even feasible. 

“The banks were incredulous: ‘You’re opening a restaurant *now*?’” Christina recalls. “And we replied, ‘Yeah, we’re opening a restaurant now.’”

Born in Glasgow, Scotland, David immigrated to the United States with his family in his early teens, where he quickly discovered his passion for the culinary arts. Shortly after high school, he enlisted in the U.S. Navy, beginning a multi-year culinary service that included a two-year tenure in the kitchen at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, cooking for President Bill Clinton at the start of his first term in 1992. Reflecting on a photograph of himself alongside the former president, David fondly recalls a favorite moment: “He told me it was the best meal he had ever eaten. I was pretty geeked about that.”

However, the Macfarlanes desired a lifestyle more conducive to family time—an arrangement ill-suited to David’s high-profile, demanding roles. They relocated several times before settling in the suburbs of Minneapolis, where David most recently worked for Fusion Culinary until his position was eliminated. While the job loss initially dismayed David, Christina viewed it as a blessing in disguise. 

“I thought, ‘Thank you, Lord! Thank you, Lord!’” she says, recognizing it as the perfect catalyst to finally pursue their shared dream.

Today, despite the economic downturn, the couple stands behind the counter of their new restaurant, *L'Ecosse*—which translates to “Scotland” in French. However, the economic climate led them to adopt a different approach to their menu than they might have under more prosperous conditions. 

“We visited over a dozen restaurants to examine menus and price points, acutely aware of the struggles in the economy,” Christina explains. 

They concluded that while patrons were still dining out, they were not seeking overly formal or lavish cuisine—the type of fare typically associated with White House state dinners. David notes that such expectations are largely a misconception anyway. 

“Comfort food,” he says. “That’s what the president wanted most.”

According to David, President Clinton’s preferred meals included simple staples like nachos and salsa, tuna sandwiches, or warm milk and cookies. “[President Clinton] wasn’t looking for any fancy, frou-frou stuff. We prepared elaborate meals for state dinners or visiting dignitaries, but at lunchtime, when the president was by himself in the Oval Office, he’d just say, ‘Lemme have a tuna sandwich.’”

At *L'Ecosse*, tuna sandwiches and warm cookies are proud menu staples. Honoring David’s Scottish heritage, the menu is largely UK-centric, featuring traditional specialties like meat pies and fish and chips. By utilizing fresh, locally sourced ingredients, performing much of the labor himself, and relying on a minimal staff, David successfully keeps operating costs down.

Currently, every item on the breakfast and lunch menus is priced under $10. The Macfarlanes plan to maintain this accessible pricing structure even when they expand to a full dinner menu following the approval of their liquor license. 

“We did that so nobody experiences sticker shock,” David says. “They are very high-quality items, but they are also inexpensive, so you aren't going to break the bank. If you want to come in and enjoy Bill Clinton's favorite lunch, it doesn't have to cost $15 during the day. We want people to understand that we relate to where they are financially.”

As Christina summarizes: “You are going to get great food—the kind your mother used to make for you.” And, ideally, the bill won't send you into debt.

counterfactuals.output:
**From State Dinners to $10 Plates: Why a White House chef is betting on cheap eats in Minneapolis**

**MINNEAPOLIS (CNN) —** On any given night five years ago, Marcus Vance might have been plating pan-seared bison with huckleberry reduction for visiting heads of state, adjusting micro-greens with tweezers under the watchful eye of Secret Service agents.

Today, his hands are just as busy, but the setting is vastly different. Inside a sunlit corner building in Northeast Minneapolis, Vance wipes down a laminate counter, hands a steaming bowl of slow-braised pork shoulder and heirloom beans to a local middle school teacher, and calls out, "Order up! That’ll be nine dollars."

Vance, 44, spent nearly a decade as a senior sous chef in the White House kitchen, serving world leaders under two presidential administrations. But last month, as high inflation and economic uncertainty continued to squeeze household budgets across the country, he traded the high-stakes politics of Washington for the frosty streets of the Midwest to open *The Public Table*. 

His mission? To prove that haute-cuisine techniques can produce a genuinely affordable meal during tough economic times.

"In Washington, I cooked for people who had everything," Vance says, adjusting his black apron over a simple gray T-shirt. "Here, I’m cooking for people who are trying to decide if they can afford to take their kids out on a Friday night. To me, this work feels a lot more urgent."

### High taste, low margin

The opening of *The Public Table* comes at a fraught moment for the restaurant industry. With food costs up, supply chains lingering in unpredictability, and consumers tightening their belts, many eateries have been forced to raise prices or close their doors. According to recent industry data, dining out has increasingly become a luxury item for the average American family.

Vance, a Minneapolis native who learned to cook at his grandmother’s side before joining the U.S. Navy and later landing at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue, saw an opportunity in the crisis. 

"When the economy dips, people don't stop wanting good food—they just stop being able to pay $30 an entree for it," Vance explains. "The challenge I set for myself was simple: How do I take French technique, hyper-local Midwestern ingredients, and presidential standards, and keep every single menu item under $12?"

The answer lies in culinary math and extreme efficiency. Vance buys "ugly" or surplus produce from local Minnesota farmers at a discount, transforms inexpensive cuts of meat through long, slow braises, and makes every sauce, stock, and loaf of bread entirely in-house. 

The menu is small—just five rotating main dishes and two sides—which eliminates food waste. On a recent Tuesday, options included a 12-hour roasted beef brisket sandwich topped with pickled local red onions ($10.50), a rich roasted squash and wild rice bowl with smoked maple vinaigrette ($8.50), and a house-made chicken noodle soup simmered with parmesan rinds ($6.00).

### "Dignity on a plate"

For local residents, the restaurant has arrived like a warm breeze in a cold winter. 

"You usually have two choices right now: fast food that costs $12 for a meal deal, or a sit-down place where lunch easily runs you $25," says Sarah Lindqvist, a nurse at a nearby hospital who stops in twice a week. "Here, the food tastes like a Michelin-star restaurant, but I can actually afford it on my paycheck."

Inside *The Public Table*, the atmosphere bridges the gap between elegance and community comfort. Framed photos of Vance at White House State Dinners hang near a chalkboard listing the day's local farmers. The seating is family-style, encouraging strangers to sit together over cheap, high-end comfort food.

Vance credits his time in the White House for teaching him discipline, but says it was his upbringing that taught him empathy. 

"A lot of chefs get caught up in ego—tweezers, edible gold, rare caviar," Vance reflects, leaning against the pass as the lunch rush begins to wane. "But the highest form of hospitality isn't serving elites. It's giving an exhausted parent a healthy, delicious meal they don't have to stress about paying for."

Economic analysts note that Vance's model, while high-risk due to slim profit margins, relies heavily on volume and community goodwill—a gamble that seems to be paying off. Since opening three weeks ago, lines have regularly stretched down the block, with the restaurant selling out of food nearly every evening.

### A bipartisan comfort

While Washington remains fiercely divided, Vance likes to joke that good, cheap food is the last truly bipartisan issue in America. 

"Democrats, Republicans, Independents—everybody wants a good meal that doesn't break the bank," Vance says with a laugh. 

As the snow begins to fall outside the window, a line of customers stretches toward the door. Vance turns back to the kitchen, scoops a ladle of fragrant, simmering stew into a bowl, and smiles. 

"I used to cook for the most powerful people in the world," he says, handing the bowl across the counter to a local mechanic. "Now I cook for the people who keep the world running. I wouldn't trade it for anything."

*L’Ecosse* (French for "Scotland"), a cozy new neighborhood spot located in the heart of the Twin Cities, officially opened its doors this week. Founded by husband-and-wife duo David and Christina Macfarlane, the restaurant offers rustic Scottish comfort food and hearty American classics with one striking catch: **every single food item on the menu costs less than $10.**

For the Macfarlanes, the price ceiling isn't just a marketing gimmick—it's a mission. 

"We look around, and we see families, students, and seniors struggling just to cover basic groceries," says Christina Macfarlane, who manages front-of-house operations and community outreach. "Eating out used to be a simple joy, but inflation has made it stressful. We wanted to build a place where anyone can walk through the door, get a hot, fresh, homemade meal, and not have to worry about their bank account."

[RELATED: How Twin Cities Restaurants Are Navigating Rising Food Costs]

### From the Highlands to the High Seas—and the White House

The culinary engine behind *L’Ecosse* is David Macfarlane, whose journey to Minneapolis is as rich as his signature gravies. Born and raised in Scotland, David learned the value of thrifty, soul-warming cooking early on, using simple, wholesome ingredients to make meals stretch. 

That philosophy served him well when he joined the Navy, eventually earning a coveted role cooking for high-ranking officials—and ultimately, President Bill Clinton. 

While catering to a sitting U.S. Commander-in-Chief might conjure images of truffle oil and caviar, David says President Clinton’s preferences leaned heavily toward the unpretentious.

"President Clinton loved good, straightforward comfort food," David recalls with a laugh. "He didn’t want fussiness. He wanted hearty soups, classic roast beef, and simple savory pies. Cooking for him taught me a valuable lesson: at the end of the day, no matter who you are—whether you're the leader of the free world or a construction worker on lunch break—people just want food that feels like a warm hug."

### Flavor on a Budget: How They Keep Prices Under $10

Maintaining a sub-$10 menu in today’s economic climate requires precision, creativity, and deep culinary experience. David draws heavily on traditional Scottish cooking, which historically relied on making the most out of humble ingredients like oats, root vegetables, and slow-cooked meats.

The menu at *L’Ecosse* features items like:
*   **The Highland Shepherd's Pie ($8.50):** Slow-braised beef and root vegetables topped with buttery mash.
*   **Traditional Scotch Broth with Fresh Bannock Bread ($6.00):** A rich lamb and barley soup served with homemade flatbread.

*   **Fish & Chips Roll ($7.50):** Crisp beer-battered fish tucked into a toasted roll with house-made tartar sauce.

By sourcing ingredients locally, reducing food waste through cross-utilization, and keeping their overhead manageable, the Macfarlanes are proving that low prices don't have to mean fast-food quality.

[RELATED: View the full opening menu for L'Ecosse here]

Local response has been overwhelmingly positive. On opening day, a line formed around the block before noon, filled with a mix of neighborhood regulars, curious foodies, and veterans drawn to David’s Navy background.

"The food is incredible, but the atmosphere is even better," said local resident Marcus Vance, holding a steaming container of stew. "You can’t even get a fast-food meal deal for under ten bucks anymore. What David and Christina are doing here takes real heart."

For the Macfarlanes, the early rush is proof that Minneapolis was hungry for more than just affordable food—it was hungry for community.

"In Scotland, hospitality isn't about luxury; it's about opening your door and offering whatever you have to a stranger," David says, wiping down the kitchen counter as the dinner rush slows. "That’s all we’re doing here. Good food, fair prices, and a warm welcome."

**From Pink Slips to Shepherd’s Pie: How One Couple Turned Job Loss Into a Neighborhood Haven**

**By Sarah Jenkins, CNN**
**PHILADELPHIA (CNN) —** The steam rising from a piping-hot plate of steak-and-ale pie smells of dark beer, slow-braised beef, and fresh thyme. But to Marcus Vance, it smells like redemption.

Just eighteen months ago, Vance, 38, was standing in the locker room of a fine-dining establishment in downtown Philadelphia, holding a manila envelope. After twelve years of grinding through 70-hour workweeks as an executive sous chef—missing birthdays, anniversaries, and holidays—he had been laid off due to corporate restructuring.

"I walked out into the afternoon sun and literally couldn't breathe," Vance recalled, wiping down a wooden table inside his new restaurant. "In the restaurant industry, your identity is wrapped up in your kitchen. Suddenly, I didn't have a kitchen. I felt completely erased."

When he arrived home that Tuesday, his wife, Claire, a 35-year-old graphic designer originally from Leeds, England, didn't panic. Instead, she put the kettle on. 

Over a pot of tea and a plate of homemade scones, the couple began to talk—not about what Marcus had lost, but about what the dining industry was missing.

### Bringing the British Pub Home

The concept was simple: authentic, British-inspired comfort food served fast, fresh, and cheap. 

Drawing on Claire’s family recipes and Marcus’s classical culinary training, the couple set out to create a menu centered on heartiness and affordability. No item on the menu would cost more than $14.

They cashed in Marcus’s modest 401(k), maxed out two credit cards, and leased a narrow, long-abandoned bakery space in Philadelphia’s Fishtown neighborhood. For four grueling months, Marcus and Claire worked late into the night—sanding floors, painting walls a cozy forest green, and sourcing second-hand kitchen equipment from closed-down diners.

"People thought we were crazy," Marcus laughed. "Opening a restaurant in this economic climate? But we weren't building a palace. We were building a living room."

When the doors opened last November, the menu was intentionally tight: classic Shepherd’s pie topped with golden, butter-whipped potatoes ($12); traditional beer-battered fish and chips served in paper with a side of mushy peas ($13); sausage rolls ($6); and warm sticky toffee pudding drenched in hot butterscotch sauce ($5).

On a recent rainy Thursday afternoon, every vintage wooden booth inside *The Humble Pie Co.* was packed. The air hummed with the clatter of silverware, the murmur of easy conversation, and the rich, buttery aroma of baking pastry.

### A Blessing in Disguise

While running a small business comes with its own brand of stress—Marcus still wakes up at 4:30 a.m. to start making the pastry dough from scratch—the couple says the ownership has given them something a fine-dining salary never could: purpose.

"When I was working in high-end kitchens, I was cooking for reviews and rich patrons who barely looked at the food," Marcus said, looking over at Claire, who was busy taking orders at the counter. "Now, I watch a tired nurse come in after a night shift, eat a bowl of hot soup and a pie, and relax. I see families laughing together."

L’Ecosse—named as a nod to Claire’s Scottish heritage and Marcus’s classical French training—has bypassed the white tablecloths in favor of a menu anchored by elevated everyday staples.

The crown jewels of their menu aren't truffle-dusted delicacies, but a $14 elevated tuna melt—made with line-caught fish, house-fermented pickles, and sharp local cheddar on sourdough—and a classic, golden-brown order of fish and chips priced at $18. 

For Claire, who manages the front-of-house and the restaurant's finances, the pivot from elite catering to neighborhood tavern was both a creative risk and a economic necessity.

"When we were writing the business plan, the economic signals were already flashing red," Claire explains, gesturing to a dining room filled with local office workers and neighborhood regulars. "If we had opened an expensive tasting-menu spot, we would be struggling to fill seats right now. Instead, we asked ourselves: What do people want when times are tough? The transition hasn't meant abandoning Marcus's high-level culinary background; rather, it has reframed it.
